title: Small things first
hookLine: practice on small grievances before big ones

lines: THE LIGHTEST WEIGHT IN THE RACK.
cards: At the end of a rack of weights in a gym sits the lightest one, small enough to lift with two fingers. It's there on purpose: muscles learn the movement on it before they're asked to carry anything heavy.
Forgiveness tends to get talked about at the heavy end of the rack: betrayal, cruelty, the things that change a life. Those are real, and they matter.
But the movement itself, noticing a hurt and letting it go, can be learned on something much lighter. Today starts at the other end of the rack.

teach.h: THE GREAT BEGINS IN THE SMALL.
teach.b: The Tao Te Ching, in its sixty-third chapter, says that the difficult things of the world are done while they are still easy, and the great things of the world while they are still small.
In Chinese, the word for small there is xi: small, fine, slender. The great begins in the small.

teach.h: FAITHFUL IN THAT WHICH IS LEAST.
teach.b: A line from Luke's Gospel says something close: "He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much." The least comes first, and it isn't wasted practice. It's where the habit forms.
And the small things are everywhere. The person who took the last coffee. The friend who was late again.
The roommate who left the dishes. The comment in the group chat that stung a little. Grievances this size come along all day, so the practice can too, several times before lunch.
Each one is a chance to run the whole motion in miniature: notice it, name it plainly, and let it go. A motion done often becomes familiar.

When something heavy does come, the movement of letting go isn't brand new; it has been rehearsed on small things, again and again. Starting small isn't a way of pretending the big wounds don't exist.
And it doesn't put them on a schedule. Not yet is still allowed for those. It just means the first rep happens on the lightest weight in the rack.

how: Some forgiveness programs suggest practicing first on minor, everyday grievances, such as a rude remark or a late friend, before working on deeper hurts.

games.why: the small one. the Tao Te Ching says great things are done while they are small, and Luke says faithful in the least is faithful in much.

practice: Find one small grievance from the last day or two, the smaller the better, a door not held, a slow checkout, and name it plainly in one sentence.
Then set it down the way you'd set down the lightest weight, without ceremony, and if another small one comes up, do the same: notice, name, release.

wordCard.voice: Xi. The Chinese word for small, fine, slender, from the Tao Te Ching's teaching that great things begin small. Today's word.
